transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... I’m here because of work, mostly. I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions. They’re deliberately planting errors in the datasets to make it look like I can’t lead the work. Which is just... I mean, I've been working in mathematical sciences for decades. I took some college courses back in the eighties, back when you actually had to understand the numbers, you know? Not like now. 

I was at the hardware store the other day and the kid at the register couldn't even make change for a twenty without the machine telling him. I was buying some weather-stripping for the front door. The drafts in the house are terrible this time of year, just completely ruins the heating bill. It's all about airflow dynamics, really. 

But anyway... my wife and the junior analysts at work, they keep trying to tell me it’s just version-control mistakes. Like a software glitch or someone syncing the files wrong. But I know what I'm looking at. They're messing with my datasets on purpose.
Aside from the issues with your files, have you ever heard voices or sounds that others around you couldn't hear?

Voices? No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear people talking when there's nobody there. Just the usual house noises, you know? 

Actually, the hum from the HVAC unit has been driving me up the wall lately. It's this low-frequency vibration, right around maybe 60 hertz, and it just carries through the floorboards right into my study where I work. I tried telling the repair guy about it—he came out last Tuesday—but he didn't even check the motor mounts. Just looked at the intake filter and charged me a hundred and fifty bucks. Can you believe that? A hundred and fifty dollars for five minutes of looking at a piece of pleated cardboard. 

It’s exactly like the mechanic I used to go to over on Elm Street. I'd go in for a simple oil change, and suddenly he's telling me I need new tie rods and a transmission flush. You really can't trust contractors these days. They just want to get in, get your money, and get out before you realize they didn't actually fix the problem. But no, to answer your question, no voices or anything. Just that damn humming.
About how long has this been going on with people tampering with your datasets at work?

Well, I've been absolutely certain about it for about two months now. That they're tracking my revisions and planting those errors, I mean. It really became obvious right around the time the weather began turning. 

Which actually reminds me, I had to get the gutters cleaned out right when all this started. You let the leaves build up in those things, and the water just pools, backs up under the shingles, and completely rots the roof deck. It's a simple volume-to-drainage ratio, but nobody thinks ahead. I hired this guy, supposed to be a professional, and he leaves his heavy aluminum ladder leaning right against my prize rhododendron. Snapped a major branch right off. I've been cultivating that bush since 2004, getting the soil pH just right—needs to be acidic, you know, right around 5.5. I use pine needles for mulch, it works wonders for the root system. 

But... what was I saying? Right, the project files. Yeah, it's been about two solid months of them sabotaging my work.

```json
{"intent": "Screen for a depressive episode to evaluate for major depressive disorder with psychotic features (F32.3)", "question": "Over these past couple of months, how

How have I been feeling? Well, honestly, I haven't really felt down or anything, if that's what you mean. I've just been focused on the work, trying to stay ahead of the errors they keep slipping in. 

But you know, speaking of feeling down, my neighbor across the street, Jim—he's been looking terrible lately. Just dragging himself out to get the paper every morning in this ratty old bathrobe. I think his son moved back in with him. The kid drives this loud, modified Honda Civic, one of those hatchbacks from the late nineties, and he parks it right on the curb, blocking the storm drain. It’s a total hazard. If we get a heavy rain, the runoff is going to pool right there, and the city won't do a damn thing about it. I tried calling public works last year about a pothole, and I was on hold for forty-five minutes before the line just went dead. Forty-five minutes! The infrastructure in this town is just crumbling, absolutely crumbling. They spend all the tax money on these fancy downtown beautification projects, planting those ornamental pear trees that smell awful in the spring, instead of fixing the roads. 

So, no, I haven't been depressed or anything. Just busy trying to keep my head above water with all the sabotage at the office.

```json
{"intent": "Screen for medical conditions or physical health changes to evaluate for psychotic disorder due to another medical condition (F06.2)", "question":

Physical health? Oh, no, I'm fine. I haven't been sick or anything. My blood pressure is right where it should be, 120 over 80, like clockwork. 

Actually, speaking of clocks, I had to take my grandfather clock in for repairs last month. It's a beautiful piece, mahogany case, German movement. Been in the family since my grandfather bought it in 1952. The pendulum was just slightly off, throwing the timing out by maybe three minutes a week. You'd think finding a horologist would be easy, but it's a dying art. The guy I found works out of this tiny shop downtown, right next to that bakery that makes those incredible sourdough loaves. You know, true sourdough needs a starter that's fed daily, it's a whole chemical process, balancing the yeast and the lactobacilli. Most places just use commercial yeast and add vinegar for the sour taste. It's a total scam. Just like those contractors I was telling you about. Everyone's cutting corners these days. 

But yeah, physically, I'm perfectly healthy. Nothing wrong with me at all.

```json
{"intent": "Screen for passivity phenomena and thought interference to differentiate schizophrenia from delusional disorder", "question": "Have you ever felt like outside forces were putting

Putting thoughts in my head? No, no, my thoughts are my own. I'm just analyzing the data, seeing the patterns they're leaving behind. Nobody is forcing thoughts into my brain or anything like that. 

Although, speaking of forces, I was reading this fascinating article the other day about magnetic fields and how they affect migratory birds. Did you know that certain species of pigeons have iron-rich structures in their beaks that act like tiny compasses? It's incredible. They can navigate thousands of miles just by sensing the Earth's magnetic pull. I used to keep homing pigeons when I was younger. Built the coop myself out of reclaimed cedar. Cedar is naturally rot-resistant, you know, much better than pine if you're not going to treat it. You have to be careful with treated lumber around animals, the chemicals they use—chromated copper arsenate, mostly, though they phased that out for residential use back in '03. Still, you never know what's leaching into the soil. That's why I only use organic compost in my vegetable garden. I grew these massive heirloom tomatoes last year, Brandywine variety. They take forever to ripen, but the flavor is just... unparalleled. 

But no, to answer your question, my thoughts are completely my own. Just my own observations about the datasets.

```json
{"intent": "Assess for a pervasive, lifelong pattern of suspiciousness and mistrust of others to differentiate paranoid personality disorder from delusional disorder", "question": "Throughout your adult life, have you

Have I always been suspicious of people? No, I wouldn't say that. I just pay attention. You know, I've always been good at noticing details that other people miss. It's just part of how my brain works, looking at the numbers, finding the anomalies. 

You know, speaking of anomalies, I was looking at my utility bill last month, and the kilowatt-hour usage spiked by almost fifteen percent compared to the same billing cycle last year. Fifteen percent! And the average temperature was actually two degrees cooler this year, so it wasn't the air conditioning. I started going through the house, checking all the appliances with a multimeter. I've got this really nice Fluke multimeter, digital, auto-ranging. It's an essential tool if you're doing any kind of electrical work. Anyway, I tested the refrigerator, the chest freezer in the garage, even the phantom draw from the television and the computer. Everything was normal. Then I realized it was the water heater. The lower heating element was failing, so the upper one was working double time to maintain the temperature. It's a dual-element system, 4500 watts each. I drained the tank, pulled the element—had to use a special socket for it, 1 and 1/16 inch, six-point—and sure enough, it was completely calcified. The hard water in this area is just brutal on appliances. I really should install a water softener, but the salt bags are so heavy, and the ion exchange process puts extra sodium in the drinking water, which isn't great for you. 

But anyway, no, I haven't spent my life not trusting people. I just trust the data. The data doesn't lie, unlike some of the people at the office.
